Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is a ubiquitous process found in a 18

variety of fields. It is of particular importance in biological sciences since it plays 19

essential and vital roles in a number of physiological and pathological processes in 20

biological systems. After LLPS, the dense droplets can grow in size via incorporating 21

solutes from surrounding environment and in some cases coalescing with other droplets. 22

Interestingly, the size of the dense droplets seems to have an upper limit but the 23


<!-- Page 4 -->


2

mechanism remains to be explored. Since the droplet size can be essential for biological 1

functioning, it is important to understand the size evolution of the phase separated 2

droplets. Here we propose a physical mechanism with consideration of impurities on the 3

surface of the dense liquid droplets. The theoretical predictions can be used to explain 4

the observations on the size evolution. Based on the coalescence mechanism, we 5

succeeded for the first time performing a challenging task, i.e., growing a single 6

suspended protein crystal via merging phase-separated droplets in a fully non-contact 7

manner. The mechanism observed may be considered as a basic model for researches in 8

much broader fields involving phase separation, such as in biology, materials science, 9

physics, chemistry, and meteorology. 10

11

1. Introduction 12

Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in biological systems became a frontier hot topic in 13

the field of life sciences in recent years 1-7. LLPS phenomenon is ubiquitous in living 14

organisms. For example, subcellular structures like membraneless organelles, 15

heterochromatin, transport channel, etc, are formed through the LLPS process 8-10. LLPS is 16

also involved in a variety of important physiological processes (for examples, gene 17

transcription 11, heterochromatin formation 8, DNA repair 12, autophagy13, spindle assembly14, 18

transcriptional regulation15, skin barrier formation 16, noise reduction in protein concentration 19

in cells 17, 18, membrane bending 19, etc.), as well as a variety of pathological processes, such 20

as Alzheimer's disease (AD) 20, 21, Parkinson's disease (PD) 22, diabetes 23, amyotrophic lateral 21

sclerosis (ALS)7, 24, 25, cancer 26, 27, leukaemic transformation 26, etc. 22

In traditional structural biology, in order to understand the function of biological 23


<!-- Page 5 -->


3

macromolecules and their complexes, it is often necessary to obtain their three-dimensional 1

atomic resolution structure, through which the functions can be understood, for example via 2

lock & key or induced-fit models. However, this approach is not applicable for the proteins 3

that have no distinct tertiary structure (intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs, about 5% of 4

total proteins in human proteome) or protein regions that are intrinsically disordered (IDRs, 5

approcx. 55% of all proteins) 27. In recent years, increasing evidences confirm that these 6

proteins play vital roles through the LLPS process, providing a new kind of interpretation for 7

the functions of biological macromolecules and their complexes simply via explaining 8

thermodynamic and kinetic processes. The new perspectives can help to better understand or 9

re-understand many physiological and pathological processes. Obviously, studying LLPS is a 10

typical example of understanding many physiological and pathological processes from the 11

perspective of physical sciences, and is providing an excellent bridge connecting physical 12

sciences and biological sciences. 13

In investigations of LLPS in biological system, the size of the dense liquid droplets is a 14

parameter of concern, because it can be essential for appropriate functioning 28, such as the 15

droplet size dependents of the rate of ribozyme cleavage 29. Further, an interesting observation 16

is that there seems to be an upper limit in the size of the dense liquid droplets after LLPS 17

depending on the type and size of the cells in which they are forming 30, 31. 18

In order to understand the size evolution phenomenon, it is necessary to study the growth 19

process of droplets. When the phase separated droplets appear in a solution, they will start to 20

grow. Droplet growth can be achieved in two ways: 1) Capture of solutes (biological 21

macromolecules) from surrounding solutions; 2) Collision and coalescence of the phase 22

separated droplets. The latter is a faster way to increase the size. Here we propose a 23


<!-- Page 6 -->


4

theoretical model for the droplet coalescence process, which can explain the phenomenon of 1

the size limit dense liquid droplets can reach. Based on the model, we assume that continuous 2

coalescence of dense liquid droplets can be achieved under sufficiently large external force 3

field, and thus a single dense liquid phase can be obtained. According to the two-step 4

nucleation theory, crystal nucleation occurs in the dense liquid phase. If a single dense liquid 5

phase can be obtained, it is hoped that the growth of a single crystal can be realized from that 6

single dense liquid. Based on this idea, we used the protein crystallization that starts from 7

LLPS as a model, and successfully realized the nucleation and growth of a single, fully 8

non-contact suspended crystal in a solution. This is a very challenging task and has never 9

been achieved before. 10

Our study, on the one hand, expounds how the dense liquid droplets grow up, explains 11

why the dense liquid droplets have an upper limit in size, and provides a new perspective for 12

understanding the phase separation phenomenon, and the droplet size evolution in biological 13

system. On the other hand, we have achieved a challenging task to grow single suspended 14

crystal in solution based on this theory, suggesting that it has strong application potential in 15

other disciplines. For example, we have found that the magnetic field influences the 16

directional migration of dense liquid droplets. This experimental fact suggests that external 17

physical fields can be used to influence the phase separation process, thus providing a 18

theoretical basis for the use of physical means in the treatment of diseases. Till now there 19

have been no reports published on the influence of external physical fields on the LLPS in 20

biological systems, but ongoing research in our laboratory, with preliminary results, reveals 21

an encouraging number of results in disease treatment via affecting LLPS using external 22

physical fields. 23

In addition to biological systems, phase separation and coalescence of liquid phases also 1

occurs in other research fields, such as materials science32-34, physics 35, chemistry36-38, etc. 2

The theory proposed in this study is also useful for understanding the phenomena found in 3

these research fields. 4

5

2. Results 6

The dense liquid phases are formed by LLPS. Theoretically, when the dense liquid 7

droplets form, they are thermodynamically stable. Further increasing the size of the droplets is 8

a process of decreasing the total free energy, thus it is an energy favourable process. If two 9

dense liquid droplets are pushed together (e.g., via Brownian motion, or purposely 10

manipulated), they may coalesce to decrease the overall free energy. 11

However, whether or not the coalescence occurs, depends on the status of the individual 12

interfaces. When many impurity particles are present on the surface of the dense liquid phases, 13

it may be difficult to realize coalescence because such impurities can prohibit direct contact 14

of the two dense liquid phases. Here we propose a model for the coalescence of dense liquids, 15

with consideration of the particles distributed at the interfaces between the dense liquid and 16

the bulk solution. Fig. 1 schematically shows the model for coalescence of dense liquid 17

droplets. 18

In a liquid system with two coexisting liquid phases, the interface between the two phases 19

will have interactions with the surrounding solute and potential impurity particles to 20

determine a contact angle due to the interfacial tensions 39 (Fig. 1a). When the contact angle 21

= 0, the impurity particles will be completely “wetting” on the interface, so that the particle 22

will tend to stay inside the dense liquid phase. While when the contact angle = 180, the 23


<!-- Page 8 -->


6

impurity particles will be completely “super-hydrophobic” at the interface, so that the 1

particles will be more likely to stay in the bulk solution. If does not equal to either 0or 2

180, the interface will tend to capture the impurity particles. In summary, the status of the 3

impurity particles at the interface will depend on the contact angle  (Fig. 1a). 4

In the theoretical model there are impurity particles distributed at the interfaces. In an 17

ideal solution, suppose there are no impurity particles, i.e., n = 0, then the force necessary for 18

a successful coalescence shall be F ≥0, which means that no or very weak external force is 19

necessary to achieve the coalescence. 20

Eq. (2) shows that, for each coalescence, the density of the impurity particles at the 21

interface will increase by 58.7% (22/3=1.587). It means that the density will sharply increase 22

after a number of coalescences. If the density is very high, the force necessary for the 23


<!-- Page 10 -->


8

coalescence will be high, so that it may be practically impossible to coalesce further 1

repeatedly (Fig. 1d). Hence we can understand why the dense droplets exhibit limited size, as 2

reported in previous publications 30, 31. In reality, the environment in the living cells is rather 3

crowded with numerous different species of macromolecules, small molecules, ions, different 4

fragments, particles, etc. These randomly moving species can be captured by the surface of 5

the dense liquid droplets, increasing the impurity particle density on the surface, thus blocking 6

the incorporation of more macromolecules into the droplets, and causing difficulties in 7

droplets coalescence. This scenario may be a partial reason why aging droplets showed 8

difficulty to coalesce 12, because aging droplets have more time to capture more impurities 9

from the surrounding environment. 10

According to the above mechanism, if we reduce the density of the impurities, or increase 11

the force for coalescing the droplets, we might be able to obtain a single large drop in the 12

solution. This scenario is quite intriguing because we can immediately think of using protein 13

crystallization as a model to test the assumption. It is well-known that LLPS occurs before 14

nucleation of protein crystals, as described in the two-step nucleation theory 40-42. In a protein 15

crystallization solution, if we can merge all the phase separated droplets to form a large one, 16

we may be able to obtain a single suspended protein crystal in the solution from that drop, in a 17

fully non-contact manner, which has never been achieved before. 18

In order to test the above concept, we used a gradient magnetic field as a tool to 19

non-contactly move and merge dense liquid droplets. To observe if magnetic fields can 20

manipulate dense liquid phases, we applied permanent magnets on a model solution 21

containing phase separated protein droplets. Since the product BB′ of magnetic field B and 22

field gradient B′ provided by a permanent magnet is low (less than 40 T2/m for a cylindrical 23

9

NdFeB magnet with dimensions 35 mm 30 mm), the magnetic force Fm, which is 1

proportional to BB′, will be small when the solution conditions are fixed. To increase the 2

magnetic force, the difference in the magnetic susceptibility between the dense liquid and 3

the bulk solution shall be large enough, which can be realized by adding a paramagnetic salt 4

to the protein solution. In this study, the paramagnetic salt MnCl2, which exhibits high 5

magnetic susceptibility, was used. 6

dense liquid droplets (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Movie 1), we clearly observed a movement of 18

which the force direction (also the movement direction of the dense liquids) is indicated. Fig. 21

As illustrated in the section above, permanent magnets can push the dense liquid droplets 10

together and can cause coalescence. This phenomenon indicated that, if the crystals nucleate 11

from the dense liquid droplets, it will be feasible to control the location and number of the 12

final crystals. To examine if it is possible to control the nucleation site, we designed an 13

apparatus with an N-N permanent magnet pair, i.e. a pair of permanent magnets with their N 14

poles facing right towards each other, and a quartz cell with a thin layer of protein 15

crystallization solution placed between the N-N poles (Fig. 2g). The geometrical arrangement 16

of the permanent magnets created a localized low magnetic field between the two N poles 17

(Fig. 2h). 18

In the case when the quartz cell was placed in the magnetic field (Fig. 2g), the crystals 19

would appear at distinct positions. According to the results of non-contact manipulation of 20

dense liquids using permanent magnets (Figs. 2e-f), we expected that the crystals would 21

appear at the localized low field zone. Our experimental observation confirmed this 22

expectation (Figs. 2i-l). It can be seen that the crystals appeared in the localized low field 23

Two proteins (hen-egg white lysozyme and proteinase K) were used as model proteins. In 8

the crystallization process of lysozyme, a visible suspended single crystal (size: ~ 0.1 mm) 9

appeared approximately 11-24 hours after starting the experiment. During the whole growth 10

process, the suspended crystal appeared to remain motionless in all experimental runs. Fig. 3c 11

shows series of images of a typical non-contact crystallization experiment of lysozyme. In 12

this experiment, we recorded both the side- and top-view videos of the crystallization process 13

for about 92 hours. The crystal first became observable (from side-view, Fig. 3c, when the 14

crystal size was 0.1 mm) after about 14 hours. The videos can be shortened for easier 15

observation (Supplementary Movie 3). More repeated experiments were performed, 16

Supplementary Movie 4 exhibited one more example of non-contact crystallization of 17

lysozyme, which was carried out for about 48 hours considering the crystal size requirement 18

for the X-ray diffraction analysis. Six times repeated experiments confirmed the same 19

phenomena. Hence we realized the non-contact crystallization of a suspended lysozyme 20

crystal using the directed magnetic force which pushed the dense liquid droplets together to 21

form a large one, and subsequently a single suspended crystal formed from that drop. 22

Supplementary Movie 6 provides an animation movie to show the process. As a comparison, 1

Supplementary Movie 7 shows an animation of crystallization under normal conditions. 2

Figs. 3e and 3f show the size evolution of lysozyme crystals grown in different conditions. 3

In the case of crystal growth in standard conditions (Fig. 3e), the crystals grew fast in the 4

beginning, after the crystals were visible, and stopped growing after several hours. In the case 5

of non-contact crystallization (Fig. 3f), it can be seen that the crystal size is linearly increasing 6

against the time after the crystal became visible, showing that the growth rate was constant 7

during the observation period. The constant growth rate indicated that the supersaturation 8

around the crystal was constant, which is a further indication that a solute depletion zone was 9

formed around the crystal. This is a good evidence to show, that the convection in the solution 10

was low or damped under such non-contact crystallization condition. Furthermore, the much 11

slower growth rate in the non-contact crystallization experiment, compared with the normal 12

case, is also in accordance assuming rather low convection. 13

In the case of proteinase K, crystallization of a non-contact single crystal was also 14

successfully achieved. Strikingly different from the seemingly motionless non-contact 15

crystallization of lysozyme, the suspended crystal of proteinase K keeps moving upward 16

during the entire growth process. For this model protein, the suspended proteinase K crystal 17

appeared about 5-10 hours after starting the experiment, and lasted for about 24 hours 18

throughout the whole crystallization experiment. Fig. 3d shows one example of the 19

time-course evolution of proteinase K crystal growth from side-view. In this example, the 20

crystal appeared at about 5 hours after starting the experiment. The recorded video was cut 21

into a shortened version (Supplementary Movie 5), from which the growth and ascending 22

process can be clearly observed. Fig. 3g shows the moved ascending distance against the time 1

since the crystal became visible from the side-view CCD camera. It can be seen that the 2

proteinase K crystal kept ascending and the movement was faster in the earlier period, and 3

later the crystal movement slowed down. 4

As mentioned above, we have observed significantly different crystallization behaviours 5

of the two proteins. In the case of lysozyme crystallization, we found that the crystal appeared 6

to remain motionless during the entire growth process, while in the case of proteinase K, the 7

crystal kept moving upward during the growth process, although the movement was rather 8

slow (approximately 2.16 mm in one day). Apparently, the movement of proteinase K crystals 9

indicated that the forces acting on the crystal changed during the growth process. 10

To identify the reason why the crystals of the two proteins behave so differently, we 11

derived the requirement (Eq. (3), refer to the Supplementary Derivation 2 for detailed 12

derivation) for keeping the crystals motionless based on the force balance in the vertical 13

direction (Fig. 3b). 14

Hence, based on the theoretical model of phase coalescence, we have achieved growing a 7

single suspended protein crystal in a fully non-contact manner. Realization of the challenging 8

task demonstrated the application potential of the model, which we believe is useful in several 9

disciplines (Fig. 4), including investigations of LLPS in both biological and physical sciences. 10

In the field of protein crystallization, there are some enigmatic phenomena. Here we will 11

explain two of them using the model proposed in this work. It was found that the 12

concentration of the protein in the crystallization solution is increasing over time at the lower 13

side of a crystallization container, and simultaneously it is decreasing at the upper side 44. 14

This phenomenon was not explained in the past, but now we understand that the phenomenon 15

is caused by phase coalescence. In the crystallization solution, phase separated droplets are 16

moving randomly due to Brownian motion, which will lead to many collisions between the 17

droplets. When two droplets collide with each other, coalescence may occur so that the 18

resulting droplets become larger. When the droplets become large enough, they will sediment 19

to the bottom of the reservoir, resulting in an increase of the protein concentration at the 20

bottom, before crystals are forming. Simultaneously, the concentration at the upper side of the 21

container will decrease. 22

According to the coalescence model, we believe that, the density of the impurity particles 1

might be high, so that coalescence events are not easy to achieve. Since a successful 2

crystallization requires that the size of the dense liquid droplets is sufficiently large, small 3

sized dense liquid droplets might not be able to form ordered nuclei, or small nulcei are 4

formed but they do not grow due to the existence of the impurities on the surface, so that the 5

crystallization solution appear clear. However, when the size of the dense liquids becomes 6

slightly larger, numerous small crystals will be observable. 7

In addition to the context of protein crystallization, the coalescence of dense liquids is also 8

frequently observed in other processes, and Eqs. (1) and (2) are useful to explain the 9

phenomena in those processes. 10

According to Eq. (1), in an ideal solution system when there are no impurities present (n = 11

0), or the impurities are completely immersed into the bulk solution (= 180) /or the dense 12

liquids (= 0), the dense liquids will coalesce after phase separation, resulting in layered 13

solutions in the gravitational field. Similarly, in the nature environment, when the 14

concentration of dust particles is nearly zero in regions with high humidity, it will be easier to 15

trigger raining via stimulation like audible sound. Therefore, in a region where the rain can be 16

produced by shouting or clapping hands, the air in that region is indicated to be very clean. 17

This phenomenon was reported as a “mysterious attraction”, e.g at the Listening Lake 18

(Tingming Lake or Miren Lake) in Yunnan Province in China. 19

In the biological systems, LLPS is now a well-known phenomenon which is found to be 20

essentially involved in many physiological and pathological processes, as described in the 21

beginning of this article 1-7. According to Eq. (1), the coalescence of dense liquids is related 22

with parameters n (the density of impurities), R (the size of the impurity), bd (the interfacial 23

tension between the bulk solution and the dense liquid), and (the contact angle between the 1

dense liquid and the impurity). Therefore, the coalescence is affected by the density of 2

impurities (n), the size of the impurities (R), and the material types, structures and properties 3

of the three phases (impurity, dense liquid, and bulk solution), which determine the 4

parameters and bd. According to this basic equation, one may theoretically foresee some 5

processes or explain the phenomena occurring in living cells during LLPS, like the examples 6

12, 45 explained before. Once rather large dense liquid droplets are observed, this may indicate 7

that the coalescence occurs fast, or the impurities in the cell, i.e. physiological products, 8

different particulate species, and other fragments, are low in quantity. In context of liquid 9

dense cluster formation more biological processes need to be studied, to provide more 10

insights about LLPS processes in the biological systems. 11

3. Conclusions 13

In this paper, we presented a theoretical model of phase coalescence to understand the 14

interesting phenomenon that the phase separated droplets after LLPS in biological system has 15

an upper limit in size. Based on the theory, we proposed a new approach using protein 16

crystallization as a model, and successfully achieved the nucleation and growth of a single 17

suspended crystal in the solution, which is a quite challenging task and has never been 18

realized before. Because LLPS plays very important roles in physiological and pathological 19

processes in biological systems, a better understanding of the physical process of LLPS is of 20

high value for related studies. The model presented in this study meet this requirement and 21

can be very helpful in further studies. Furthermore, a very important implication can be 22

inferred from the experimental fact that external physical fields can affect LLPS process. In 23


<!-- Page 25 -->


23

other words, the phenomenon can provide theoretical basis for the utilization of external 1

physical fields in influencing LLPS and hence in treatments of LLPS related diseases. 2

In research fields other than biological sciences, LLPS is also a ubiquitous phenomenon 3

and phase coalescence occurs in many chemical processes. The theoretical model proposed in 4

this study can therefore be also useful for studying LLPS processes in these fields (materials 5

science, physics, chemistry, meteorology, etc.). 6
